title: Die Nixe im Teich
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 181. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, Thür, Rath, Reichthum).
about: A struggling miller strikes a bargain with a water-spirit for sudden wealth, without grasping that the price is whatever has just been born in his house — his own newborn son. The story then leaps forward to the son’s adulthood, when the nixie tries to claim him after all, and an old woman’s counsel becomes the means of his and his wife’s escape. Moonlight and water carry much of the atmosphere in the second half.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Müller, der führte mit seiner Frau ein vergnügtes Leben.
sentences.l: There was once a miller who led a contented life with his wife.
sentences.i: There was once a miller, and he led a contented life with his wife.
sentences.n: “Es war einmal” — the standing opening of these tales; the es is only a placeholder, which lets the miller come after the verb. “der führte” carries on with a demonstrative rather than a relative pronoun: ‘that one led’, a very common old turn.

sentences.t: Sie hatten Geld und Gut, und ihr Wohlstand nahm von Jahr zu Jahr noch zu.
sentences.l: They had money and goods, and their prosperity increased still from year to year.
sentences.i: They had money and property, and their prosperity grew greater still from year to year.
sentences.n: “Geld und Gut” is a fixed pair: das Gut here is property, the noun, not the adjective gut, ‘good’. “zunehmen” is separable — nahm … zu.

sentences.t: Aber Unglück kommt über Nacht: wie ihr Reichthum gewachsen war, so schwand er von Jahr zu Jahr wieder hin, und zuletzt konnte der Müller kaum noch die Mühle, in der er saß, sein Eigenthum nennen.
sentences.l: But misfortune comes overnight: as their riches had grown, so it dwindled away again from year to year, and at last the miller could scarcely call the mill in which he sat his property.
sentences.i: But misfortune comes overnight: as their wealth had grown, so it dwindled away again from year to year, until at last the miller could hardly call the mill he sat in his own.
sentences.n: The present tense of “Unglück kommt über Nacht” steps out of the story to state a general truth, the way a proverb does. “wie …, so …” gives the rise and the fall the same shape. “hinschwinden” — to dwindle away; Reichthum and Eigenthum carry the 1857 -th-.

sentences.t: Er war voll Kummer, und wenn er sich nach der Arbeit des Tags nieder legte, so fand er keine Ruhe, sondern wälzte sich voll Sorgen in seinem Bett.
sentences.l: He was full of grief, and when he laid himself down after the work of the day, he found no rest, but tossed full of cares in his bed.
sentences.i: He was full of grief, and when he lay down after the day’s work he found no rest, but tossed in his bed with worry.
sentences.n: “sich nieder legen” — to lay oneself down; German makes lying down reflexive, and nieder stands apart from the verb. “des Tags” is a genitive of time, the day’s work.

sentences.t: Eines Morgens stand er schon vor Tagesanbruch auf, gieng hinaus ins Freie und dachte es sollte ihm leichter ums Herz werden.
sentences.l: One morning he got up already before daybreak, went out into the open and thought it should grow lighter about his heart.
sentences.i: One morning he rose before daybreak, went out into the open air, and thought his heart would grow lighter.
sentences.n: “Eines Morgens” is another genitive of time. “ins Freie” — out into the open, das Freie being the open country. “es wird einem leichter ums Herz” is the standing phrase for spirits lifting; German puts the lightness around the heart.

sentences.t: Als er über dem Mühldamm dahin schritt, brach eben der erste Sonnenstrahl hervor, und er hörte in dem Weiher etwas rauschen.
sentences.l: As he strode along over the mill-dam, the first ray of sun just broke forth, and he heard something rushing in the pond.
sentences.i: As he strode along over the mill-dam, the first ray of sun broke through, and he heard something stirring in the pond.
sentences.n: “hervorbrechen” — to break forth; separable, brach … hervor. “rauschen” is a bare infinitive after hören: he heard something rush, the sound moving water makes.

sentences.t: Er wendete sich um und erblickte ein schönes Weib, das sich langsam aus dem Wasser erhob.
sentences.l: He turned himself around and caught sight of a beautiful woman who was rising slowly out of the water.
sentences.i: He turned round and caught sight of a beautiful woman rising slowly out of the water.
sentences.n: “sich umwenden” — to turn round, with the particle um at the end. Weib is the older plain word for a woman and carries none of the contempt it took on later.

sentences.t: Ihre langen Haare, die sie über den Schultern mit ihren zarten Händen gefaßt hatte, flossen an beiden Seiten herab und bedeckten ihren weißen Leib.
sentences.l: Her long hair, which she had gathered over her shoulders with her delicate hands, flowed down on both sides and covered her white body.
sentences.n: German says die Haare, plural, where English has one word for a whole head of hair. “fließen” of hair is the ordinary picture of it falling, and “herab” gives the direction, downward toward us.

sentences.t: Er sah wohl daß es die Nixe des Teichs war und wußte vor Furcht nicht ob er davon gehen oder stehen bleiben sollte.
sentences.l: He saw well that it was the nixie of the pond, and for fear he did not know whether he should go away or stay standing.
sentences.i: He saw well enough that it was the nixie of the pond, and for fear he did not know whether to go away or to stand still.
sentences.n: A Nixe is a water-sprite, female, who lives in a pond or river and lays claim to whatever comes near it. “vor Furcht” — for fear, vor giving the cause. Both “davon gehen” and “stehen bleiben” are printed as two words here.

sentences.t: Aber die Nixe ließ ihre sanfte Stimme hören, nannte ihn bei Namen und fragte warum er so traurig wäre.
sentences.l: But the nixie let her soft voice be heard, called him by name and asked why he was so sad.
sentences.i: But the nixie let her gentle voice be heard, called him by his name, and asked why he was so sad.
sentences.n: “ließ … hören” is lassen with an infinitive: let her voice be heard. “wäre” is the subjunctive of reported speech — her question given as report, marked in the verb rather than by quotation.

sentences.t: Der Müller war anfangs verstummt, als er sie aber so freundlich sprechen hörte, faßte er sich ein Herz und erzählte ihr daß er sonst in Glück und Reichthum gelebt hätte, aber jetzt so arm wäre, daß er sich nicht zu rathen wüßte.
sentences.l: The miller was struck dumb at first, but when he heard her speak so kindly, he took a heart to himself and told her that he had once lived in fortune and riches, but was now so poor that he did not know how to counsel himself.
sentences.i: At first the miller was struck dumb, but when he heard her speak so kindly he took heart, and told her that he had once lived in fortune and wealth but was now so poor that he was at his wits’ end.
sentences.n: “sich ein Herz fassen” — to take a heart to oneself, to pluck up courage. “sich nicht zu rathen wissen” is to know no counsel for oneself, to be at a loss. Three subjunctives in a row — hätte, wäre, wüßte — keep the whole account in his voice rather than the tale’s.

sentences.t: „Sei ruhig,“ antwortete die Nixe, „ich will dich reicher und glücklicher machen als du je gewesen bist, nur mußt du mir versprechen daß du mir geben willst was eben in deinem Hause jung geworden ist.“
sentences.l: “Be calm,” answered the nixie, “I will make you richer and more fortunate than you have ever been, only you must promise me that you will give me what has just become young in your house.”
sentences.i: “Be easy,” answered the nixie. “I will make you richer and luckier than you have ever been, only you must promise me to give me what has just been born in your house.”
sentences.n: “was eben jung geworden ist” — what has just become young: a deliberately blank phrase that would cover a litter of pups, and the miller hears it that way. Note the du — she is familiar with him from the first word.

sentences.t: „Was kann das anders sein,“ dachte der Müller, „als ein junger Hund oder ein junges Kätzchen?“ und sagte ihr zu was sie verlangte.
sentences.l: “What can that be other,” thought the miller, “than a young dog or a young kitten?” and he promised her what she demanded.
sentences.i: “What can that be,” thought the miller, “but a puppy or a kitten?” and he promised her what she asked.
sentences.n: “zusagen” — to promise, to pledge; separable, sagte … zu, and much firmer than plain sagen. His question answers itself, which is exactly the trap.

sentences.t: Die Nixe stieg wieder in das Wasser hinab, und er eilte getröstet und gutes Muthes nach seiner Mühle.
sentences.l: The nixie climbed down into the water again, and he hurried, comforted and of good courage, to his mill.
sentences.i: The nixie sank down into the water again, and he hurried home to his mill, comforted and in good heart.
sentences.n: “gutes Muthes” is an old genitive of manner — of good courage, in good spirits; Muth is the 1857 spelling of Mut.

sentences.t: Noch hatte er sie nicht erreicht, da trat die Magd aus der Hausthüre und rief ihm zu er sollte sich freuen, seine Frau hätte ihm einen kleinen Knaben geboren.
sentences.l: He had not yet reached it when the maid stepped out of the house door and called to him he should be glad, his wife had borne him a little boy.
sentences.i: He had not yet reached it when the maid stepped out of the house door and called to him that he should be glad: his wife had borne him a little boy.
sentences.n: “Noch hatte er sie nicht erreicht” puts the verb first and holds the sentence in suspense; the “da” answers it — hardly had he, when. “hätte … geboren” is once more the subjunctive of report, the maid’s news in the maid’s mouth.

sentences.t: Der Müller stand wie vom Blitz gerührt, er sah wohl daß die tückische Nixe das gewußt und ihn betrogen hatte.
sentences.l: The miller stood as if touched by lightning; he saw well that the malicious nixie had known that and had deceived him.
sentences.i: The miller stood as if struck by lightning; he saw well enough that the treacherous nixie had known it and had cheated him.
sentences.n: “wie vom Blitz gerührt” — as if touched by lightning; gerührt is the quiet word ‘touched’, which makes the German gentler than a blow. “tückisch” is malicious in a hidden, sly way.

sentences.t: Mit gesenktem Haupt trat er zu dem Bett seiner Frau, und als sie ihn fragte „warum freust du dich nicht über den schönen Knaben?“ so erzählte er ihr was ihm begegnet war und was für ein Versprechen er der Nixe gegeben hatte.
sentences.l: With sunken head he stepped to his wife’s bed, and when she asked him “why do you not rejoice over the beautiful boy?” he told her what had happened to him and what kind of promise he had given the nixie.
sentences.i: With his head bowed he went to his wife’s bed, and when she asked him, “Why are you not glad of the beautiful boy?” he told her what had befallen him and what promise he had given the nixie.
sentences.n: “sich freuen über” — to be glad about a thing. “begegnen” takes the dative and means simply to happen to someone. “was für ein” = what sort of a, as elsewhere in these tales.

sentences.t: „Was hilft mir Glück und Reichthum,“ fügte er hinzu, „wenn ich mein Kind verlieren soll? aber was kann ich thun?“
sentences.l: “What use to me are fortune and riches,” he added, “if I am to lose my child? but what can I do?”
sentences.i: “What good are fortune and wealth to me,” he added, “if I am to lose my child? But what can I do?”
sentences.n: “hinzufügen” — to add; separable, fügte … hinzu. “Was hilft mir …?” is literally ‘what helps me’, the ordinary way of asking what use a thing is.

sentences.t: Auch die Verwandten, die herbeigekommen waren, Glück zu wünschen, wußten keinen Rath.
sentences.l: Even the relatives, who had come up to wish him joy, knew no counsel.
sentences.i: Even the relatives who had come to wish him joy knew of no remedy.
sentences.n: “Glück wünschen” — to wish someone joy, the phrase for congratulation at a birth. “keinen Rath wissen” is to know of no way out; Rath is the 1857 spelling of Rat.

sentences.t: Indessen kehrte das Glück in das Haus des Müllers wieder ein.
sentences.l: Meanwhile fortune turned in again at the miller’s house.
sentences.i: Meanwhile good fortune came back into the miller’s house.
sentences.n: “einkehren” — to turn in and stay, as a traveller turns in at an inn; separable, kehrte … ein. “Indessen” is ‘meanwhile’.

sentences.t: Was er unternahm gelang, es war als ob Kisten und Kasten von selbst sich füllten und das Geld im Schrank über Nacht sich mehrte.
sentences.l: What he undertook succeeded; it was as if chests and boxes filled themselves of their own accord and the money in the cupboard multiplied itself overnight.
sentences.i: Whatever he undertook succeeded; it was as if chests and boxes filled of themselves and the money in the cupboard multiplied overnight.
sentences.n: “Kisten und Kasten” is a set pair for all one’s boxes and chests, kept here as the doublet it is. “als ob” takes the subjunctive — füllten, mehrte are what it seemed like, not what the tale claims.

sentences.t: Es dauerte nicht lange, so war sein Reichthum größer als je zuvor.
sentences.l: It did not last long, and his riches were greater than ever before.
sentences.i: It was not long before his wealth was greater than ever before.
sentences.n: “Es dauerte nicht lange, so …” is a standing frame: it did not last long, and then. German joins the halves with so where English uses ‘before’.

sentences.t: Aber er konnte sich nicht ungestört darüber freuen: die Zusage, die er der Nixe gethan hatte, quälte sein Herz.
sentences.l: But he could not rejoice over it undisturbed: the promise that he had made to the nixie tormented his heart.
sentences.i: But he could not take undisturbed joy in it: the promise he had given the nixie tormented his heart.
sentences.n: “eine Zusage thun” — to give a pledge; thun is the 1857 spelling of tun. The noun Zusage picks up the verb zusagen from the bargain at the pond.

sentences.t: So oft er an dem Teich vorbei kam, fürchtete er sie möchte auftauchen und ihn an seine Schuld mahnen.
sentences.l: As often as he came past the pond, he feared she might surface and remind him of his debt.
sentences.i: Every time he came past the pond, he feared she might rise up and put him in mind of his debt.
sentences.n: “Schuld” is at once a debt and a guilt, and the tale needs both senses. “an etwas mahnen” is what a creditor does — to press for what is owed.

sentences.t: Den Knaben selbst ließ er nicht in die Nähe des Wassers: „hüte dich,“ sagte er zu ihm, „wenn du das Wasser berührst, so kommt eine Hand heraus, hascht dich und zieht dich hinab.“
sentences.l: The boy himself he did not let near the water: “guard yourself,” he said to him, “if you touch the water, a hand comes out, snatches you and draws you down.”
sentences.i: The boy himself he never let near the water. “Take care,” he said to him; “if you touch the water, a hand will come out, snatch you, and drag you down.”
sentences.n: “hascht” is from haschen, to snatch or seize — a hunting word, and it will come literally true. “sich hüten” is to be on one’s guard. The father’s warning is the whole plot in three verbs.

sentences.t: Doch als Jahr auf Jahr vergieng, und die Nixe sich nicht wieder zeigte, so fieng der Müller an sich zu beruhigen.
sentences.l: Yet as year upon year passed and the nixie did not show herself again, the miller began to grow easy.
sentences.i: Yet as year followed year and the nixie did not show herself again, the miller began to grow easy in his mind.
sentences.n: “anfangen” splits wide open here — “fieng … an”, with the whole infinitive phrase in between; fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing, and vergieng of verging.

sentences.t: Der Knabe wuchs zum Jüngling heran und kam bei einem Jäger in die Lehre.
sentences.l: The boy grew up into a youth and came to a huntsman as an apprentice.
sentences.i: The boy grew up into a young man and was apprenticed to a huntsman.
sentences.n: “heranwachsen” — to grow up; separable, wuchs … heran. “in die Lehre kommen” is the settled phrase for being taken on as an apprentice, die Lehre being the apprenticeship itself rather than a lesson.

sentences.t: Als er ausgelernt hatte und ein tüchtiger Jäger geworden war, nahm ihn der Herr des Dorfes in seine Dienste.
sentences.l: When he had learned out and had become a capable huntsman, the lord of the village took him into his service.
sentences.i: When he had served out his time and become a capable huntsman, the lord of the village took him into his service.
sentences.n: “auslernen” — to finish one’s apprenticeship; there is no neat English verb for it, and ‘learned out’ is what the German says. “in Dienste nehmen” — to take into service.

sentences.t: In dem Dorf war ein schönes und treues Mädchen, das gefiel dem Jäger, und als sein Herr das bemerkte, schenkte er ihm ein kleines Haus; die beiden hielten Hochzeit, lebten ruhig und glücklich und liebten sich von Herzen.
sentences.l: In the village there was a beautiful and faithful girl; she pleased the huntsman, and when his lord noticed that, he gave him a little house; the two held their wedding, lived quietly and happily and loved each other from the heart.
sentences.i: In the village there was a beautiful and faithful girl, and she pleased the huntsman; when his lord saw it, he made him a present of a little house. The two held their wedding, lived quietly and happily, and loved each other from their hearts.
sentences.n: “gefallen” takes the dative: the girl pleases to the huntsman, where English says he liked her. “das” refers back to the girl although Mädchen is grammatically neuter — German follows the grammar and not the person.

sentences.t: Einsmals verfolgte der Jäger ein Reh.
sentences.l: One time the huntsman pursued a roe.
sentences.i: One day the huntsman was following a roe deer.
sentences.n: “Einsmals” is an old form of einmal, on one occasion — the tale’s way of opening a new turn of events.

sentences.t: Als das Thier aus dem Wald in das freie Feld ausbog, setzte er ihm nach und streckte es endlich mit einem Schuß nieder.
sentences.l: When the animal swerved out of the wood into the open field, he set after it and finally struck it down with a shot.
sentences.i: When the beast broke out of the wood into the open field, he set after it and at last brought it down with a shot.
sentences.n: Three separable verbs in a row, each with its particle waiting at the end of its clause: “ausbiegen”, to swerve out; “nachsetzen”, to set after in pursuit; “niederstrecken”, to stretch down, that is to bring down.

sentences.t: Er bemerkte nicht daß er sich in der Nähe des gefährlichen Weihers befand, und gieng, nachdem er das Thier ausgeweidet hatte, zu dem Wasser, um seine mit Blut befleckten Hände zu waschen.
sentences.l: He did not notice that he was in the neighbourhood of the dangerous pond, and went, after he had gutted the animal, to the water in order to wash his hands, which were stained with blood.
sentences.i: He did not notice that he was near the dangerous pond, and after he had gutted the beast he went to the water to wash his blood-stained hands.
sentences.n: “sich befinden” — to find oneself somewhere, simply to be there. “mit Blut befleckten” stands before its noun as one long adjective, a build German manages easily and English must unpack. “ausweiden” is the hunter’s word for drawing a carcass.

sentences.t: Kaum aber hatte er sie hinein getaucht, als die Nixe emporstieg, lachend mit ihren nassen Armen ihn umschlang und so schnell hinabzog, daß die Wellen über ihm zusammenschlugen.
sentences.l: But hardly had he dipped them in when the nixie rose up, laughing wound her wet arms about him and drew him down so quickly that the waves closed together over him.
sentences.i: But hardly had he dipped them in when the nixie rose up, laughing, wound her wet arms about him, and drew him down so quickly that the waves closed over him.
sentences.n: “Kaum hatte er …, als …” — hardly had he, when; the verb comes first because kaum stands ahead of it. The laugh is the tale’s only comment on her, and no explanation of it is offered here or later.

sentences.t: Als es Abend war und der Jäger nicht nach Haus kam, so gerieth seine Frau in Angst.
sentences.l: When it was evening and the huntsman did not come home, his wife fell into fear.
sentences.i: When evening came and the huntsman did not come home, his wife grew afraid.
sentences.n: “in Angst gerathen” — to fall into fear; gerathen is the 1857 spelling of geraten, used of coming into a state, generally against one’s will.

sentences.t: Sie gieng aus ihn zu suchen, und da er ihr oft erzählt hatte daß er sich vor den Nachstellungen der Nixe in Acht nehmen müßte und nicht in die Nähe des Weihers sich wagen dürfte, so ahnte sie schon was geschehen war.
sentences.l: She went out to seek him, and since he had often told her that he must be on his guard against the nixie’s snares and might not venture near the pond, she already guessed what had happened.
sentences.i: She went out to look for him, and since he had often told her that he had to be on his guard against the nixie’s snares and might not venture near the pond, she already guessed what had happened.
sentences.n: “sich in Acht nehmen vor” — to be on one’s guard against. “sich wagen” is to venture oneself somewhere: the verb wagen, to dare, and not der Wagen, a cart. Nachstellungen are the traps and lyings-in-wait of a pursuer.

sentences.t: Sie eilte zu dem Wasser, und als sie am Ufer seine Jägertasche liegen fand, da konnte sie nicht länger an dem Unglück zweifeln.
sentences.l: She hurried to the water, and when she found his game-bag lying on the bank, then she could no longer doubt the misfortune.
sentences.i: She hurried to the water, and when she found his game-bag lying on the bank she could no longer doubt the misfortune.
sentences.n: “liegen fand” — found it lying; German puts a bare infinitive with finden where English uses the -ing form. “an etwas zweifeln” — to doubt a thing, with an.

sentences.t: Wehklagend und händeringend rief sie ihren Liebsten mit Namen, aber vergeblich:
sentences.l: Wailing and hand-wringing she called her beloved by name, but in vain:
sentences.i: Wailing and wringing her hands, she called her beloved by name, but in vain:
sentences.n: Two participles compounded into single words — “wehklagend” from Weh and klagen, “händeringend” from Hände and ringen. German builds them freely; English needs a phrase for the second.

sentences.t: sie eilte hinüber auf die andere Seite des Weihers, und rief ihn aufs neue:
sentences.l: she hurried over to the other side of the pond, and called him anew:
sentences.i: she hurried across to the other side of the pond and called him again:
sentences.n: “aufs neue” — anew, afresh (aufs = auf das). The colons string her three attempts together as one unbroken movement; the tale refuses to divide them into sentences.

sentences.t: sie schalt die Nixe mit harten Worten, aber keine Antwort erfolgte.
sentences.l: she scolded the nixie with hard words, but no answer followed.
sentences.i: she railed at the nixie with hard words, but no answer came.
sentences.n: “schalt” is the past of schelten, to scold, a strong verb that changes its vowel without warning. “erfolgen” is the formal word for something ensuing, and its flatness is the point: nothing does.

sentences.t: Der Spiegel des Wassers blieb ruhig, nur das halbe Gesicht des Mondes blickte unbeweglich zu ihr herauf.
sentences.l: The mirror of the water stayed calm; only the half face of the moon looked up motionless at her.
sentences.i: The surface of the water stayed calm; only the half face of the moon looked up at her, motionless.
sentences.n: “der Spiegel des Wassers” — the water’s mirror, German’s ordinary picture for a still surface. The moon looks up because it is the reflection she sees; the moon keeps this part all through the tale, and only when it is full does anything move.

sentences.t: Die arme Frau verließ den Teich nicht.
sentences.l: The poor woman did not leave the pond.
sentences.n: A short flat sentence after the long ones: the tale slows to the pace of her watching.

sentences.t: Mit schnellen Schritten, ohne Rast und Ruhe, umkreißte sie ihn immer von neuem, manchmal still, manchmal einen heftigen Schrei ausstoßend, manchmal in leisem Wimmern.
sentences.l: With quick steps, without rest and repose, she circled it again and again, sometimes silent, sometimes uttering a violent cry, sometimes in soft whimpering.
sentences.i: With quick steps, without rest or pause, she circled it again and again, sometimes silent, sometimes uttering a wild cry, sometimes in soft whimpering.
sentences.n: “Rast und Ruhe” is a fixed pair, rest and repose. “ausstoßend” is a present participle standing in a list where English would sooner use a finite verb; the three “manchmal” phrases are held deliberately parallel.

sentences.t: Endlich waren ihre Kräfte zu Ende: sie sank zur Erde nieder und verfiel in einen tiefen Schlaf.
sentences.l: At last her strengths were at an end: she sank down to the earth and fell into a deep sleep.
sentences.i: At last her strength was at an end: she sank down to the ground and fell into a deep sleep.
sentences.n: German has Kräfte in the plural, the several powers of the body, where English has one strength. “niedersinken” splits — sank … nieder; “verfallen in” is to fall into a state one does not choose.

sentences.t: Bald überkam sie ein Traum.
sentences.l: Soon a dream came over her.
sentences.i: Soon a dream came upon her.
sentences.n: “überkommen” — to come over someone. The dream is the subject and she the object: in German the dream is the one that acts.

sentences.t: Sie stieg zwischen großen Felsblöcken angstvoll aufwärts; Dornen und Ranken hakten sich an ihre Füße, der Regen schlug ihr ins Gesicht und der Wind zauste ihr langes Haar.
sentences.l: She climbed upward, full of fear, between great blocks of rock; thorns and tendrils hooked themselves on her feet, the rain beat into her face and the wind tugged at her long hair.
sentences.i: Full of fear she climbed upward between great blocks of rock; thorns and creepers caught at her feet, the rain beat in her face, and the wind tore at her long hair.
sentences.n: “schlug ihr ins Gesicht” — the dative ihr says whose face it is; German rarely uses a possessive where the person can stand in the dative. “sich haken an” is to catch, to hook onto.

sentences.t: Als sie die Anhöhe erreicht hatte, bot sich ein ganz anderer Anblick dar.
sentences.l: When she had reached the height, a quite different sight presented itself.
sentences.i: When she had reached the top of the rise, a wholly different scene presented itself.
sentences.n: “sich darbieten” — to present itself; separable, and the particle dar (an old word for ‘forth, there’) waits at the very end. This is the High German prefix dar-, not the Low German dar meaning ‘there’ that turns up in the northern tales.

sentences.t: Der Himmel war blau, die Luft mild, der Boden senkte sich sanft hinab und auf einer grünen, bunt beblümten Wiese stand eine reinliche Hütte.
sentences.l: The sky was blue, the air mild, the ground sloped gently down, and on a green meadow, many-coloured with flowers, stood a neat little hut.
sentences.i: The sky was blue, the air mild, the ground sloped gently away, and on a green meadow bright with flowers stood a neat little hut.
sentences.n: “die Luft mild” drops the verb again, carrying ‘was’ over from the first clause. “bunt beblümt” — flowered in many colours, a compound made on the spot, as German does at will. “reinlich” is trim and well kept rather than merely clean.

sentences.t: Sie gieng darauf zu und öffnete die Thüre, da saß eine Alte mit weißen Haaren, die ihr freundlich winkte.
sentences.l: She went up to it and opened the door; there sat an old woman with white hair, who beckoned to her kindly.
sentences.n: “eine Alte” is the adjective alt used as a noun, and feminine: the old woman. The same form with der would be an old man. “zugehen auf” splits — “gieng darauf zu”.

sentences.t: In dem Augenblick erwachte die arme Frau.
sentences.l: In that moment the poor woman awoke.
sentences.n: The dream breaks off on the threshold: she has seen the beckoning and nothing beyond it.

sentences.t: Der Tag war schon angebrochen, und sie entschloß sich gleich dem Traum Folge zu leisten.
sentences.l: The day had already broken, and she resolved at once to give the dream compliance.
sentences.i: The day had already broken, and she resolved at once to do as the dream had shown her.
sentences.n: “Folge leisten” with the dative — to comply with, to act upon; Folge here is the noun ‘following’, not the imperative of folgen. “anbrechen” of the day is to break, as in English.

sentences.t: Sie stieg mühsam den Berg hinauf, und es war alles so, wie sie es in der Nacht gesehen hatte.
sentences.l: She climbed the mountain up laboriously, and everything was just as she had seen it in the night.
sentences.i: She climbed the mountain laboriously, and everything was just as she had seen it in the night.
sentences.n: “hinauf” gives the direction and stands at the end: climbed the mountain — up. “mühsam” is with Mühe, with toil.

sentences.t: Die Alte empfieng sie freundlich und zeigte ihr einen Stuhl, auf den sie sich setzen sollte.
sentences.l: The old woman received her kindly and showed her a chair on which she should sit down.
sentences.i: The old woman received her kindly and pointed out a chair for her to sit down on.
sentences.n: “empfieng” is the 1857 spelling of empfing (empfangen). The relative clause keeps its preposition at the front — “auf den”, on which — where English leaves ‘on’ at the end.

sentences.t: „Du mußt ein Unglück erlebt haben,“ sagte sie, „weil du meine einsame Hütte aufsuchst.“
sentences.l: “You must have lived through a misfortune,” she said, “since you seek out my lonely hut.”
sentences.i: “You must have met with some misfortune,” she said, “since you seek out my lonely hut.”
sentences.n: “weil” here gives the ground for a guess rather than the cause of an event: she reasons backward from the visit. “aufsuchen” — to seek out, to go looking for.

sentences.t: Die Frau erzählte ihr unter Thränen was ihr begegnet war.
sentences.l: The woman told her under tears what had happened to her.
sentences.i: In tears, the woman told her what had befallen her.
sentences.n: “unter Thränen” — literally under tears, German’s way of saying amid weeping; Thränen carries the 1857 -th-.

sentences.t: „Tröste dich,“ sagte die Alte, „ich will dir helfen: da hast du einen goldenen Kamm.
sentences.l: “Comfort yourself,” said the old woman, “I will help you: there you have a golden comb.
sentences.i: “Take comfort,” said the old woman, “I will help you: here is a golden comb.
sentences.n: “da hast du” is what one says while handing a thing over — there you are. This is the first of the three golden objects; each will be given, used at the full moon, and carried off by a wave.

sentences.t: Harre bis der Vollmond aufgestiegen ist, dann geh zu dem Weiher, setze dich am Rand nieder und strähle dein langes schwarzes Haar mit diesem Kamm.
sentences.l: Wait until the full moon has risen, then go to the pond, set yourself down at the edge and comb out your long black hair with this comb.
sentences.i: Wait until the full moon has risen, then go to the pond, sit down at the edge, and comb out your long black hair with this comb.
sentences.n: “harren” is an old and elevated word for waiting. “strählen” is to comb, from der Strähl, a comb — long dead in modern German, which uses kämmen, the very verb the tale itself reaches for a few lines later.

sentences.t: Wenn du aber fertig bist, so lege ihn am Ufer nieder, und du wirst sehen was geschieht.“
sentences.l: But when you are finished, then lay it down on the bank, and you will see what happens.
sentences.i: But when you have finished, lay it down on the bank, and you will see what happens.
sentences.n: “niederlegen” splits: lege … nieder. The old woman never says what will happen, and the same closing words end all three of her instructions.

sentences.t: Die Frau kehrte zurück, aber die Zeit bis zum Vollmond verstrich ihr langsam.
sentences.l: The woman returned, but the time until the full moon passed slowly for her.
sentences.i: The woman went back, but the time until the full moon passed slowly for her.
sentences.n: “verstrich ihr” — the dative ihr says for whom it passed slowly. “zurückkehren” splits: kehrte … zurück.

sentences.t: Endlich erschien die leuchtende Scheibe am Himmel, da gieng sie hinaus an den Weiher, setzte sich nieder und kämmte ihre langen schwarzen Haare mit dem goldenen Kamm, und als sie fertig war, legte sie ihn an den Rand des Wassers nieder.
sentences.l: At last the shining disc appeared in the sky; then she went out to the pond, sat herself down and combed her long black hair with the golden comb, and when she was finished, she laid it down at the edge of the water.
sentences.i: At last the shining disc appeared in the sky. Then she went out to the pond, sat down, and combed her long black hair with the golden comb; and when she had finished, she laid it down at the edge of the water.
sentences.n: “die leuchtende Scheibe” — the shining disc, that is the full moon; a Scheibe is any flat round thing, a disc or a pane of glass. The sentence carries out the instruction almost word for word, as these tales like to do.

sentences.t: Nicht lange, so brauste es aus der Tiefe, eine Welle erhob sich, rollte an das Ufer und führte den Kamm mit sich fort.
sentences.l: Not long, and there was a roaring out of the deep; a wave rose up, rolled to the bank and carried the comb away with it.
sentences.i: It was not long before a roaring came out of the deep: a wave rose, rolled to the bank, and carried the comb away with it.
sentences.n: “brauste es” — the impersonal es, with nobody doing the roaring; German can leave the agent out entirely. “die Tiefe” here is the noun, the deep, not the adjective tief. “fortführen” splits: führte … fort.

sentences.t: Es dauerte nicht länger als der Kamm nöthig hatte, auf den Grund zu sinken, so theilte sich der Wasserspiegel und der Kopf des Jägers stieg in die Höhe.
sentences.l: It lasted no longer than the comb needed to sink to the bottom, and the water’s mirror parted and the head of the huntsman rose up on high.
sentences.i: It took no longer than the comb needed to sink to the bottom: the surface of the water parted, and the huntsman’s head rose up.
sentences.n: “nöthig haben” — to need; nöthig is the 1857 spelling of nötig. “sich theilen” is to part, to divide itself: the water acts upon itself, as the wave did.

sentences.t: Er sprach nicht, schaute aber seine Frau mit traurigen Blicken an.
sentences.l: He did not speak, but looked at his wife with sad glances.
sentences.i: He did not speak, but looked at his wife with sorrowful eyes.
sentences.n: “anschauen” — to look at; separable, and the particle an waits to the very end of the clause, behind everything else.

sentences.t: In demselben Augenblick kam eine zweite Welle herangerauscht und bedeckte das Haupt des Mannes.
sentences.l: In the same moment a second wave came rushing up and covered the head of the man.
sentences.i: At that same moment a second wave came rushing up and covered the man’s head.
sentences.n: “kam herangerauscht” — came rushing up; German joins a past participle to kommen to say how a thing arrived. Haupt is the elevated word for a head, kept here for the man himself.

sentences.t: Alles war verschwunden, der Weiher lag so ruhig wie zuvor und nur das Gesicht des Vollmondes glänzte darauf.
sentences.l: Everything was vanished, the pond lay so calm as before and only the face of the full moon gleamed upon it.
sentences.i: Everything had vanished; the pond lay as calm as before, and only the face of the full moon shone on it.
sentences.n: The scene shuts exactly as it opened, with the moon’s face on the water: the first attempt has changed nothing.

sentences.t: Trostlos kehrte die Frau zurück, doch der Traum zeigte ihr die Hütte der Alten.
sentences.l: Disconsolate the woman returned, but the dream showed her the old woman’s hut.
sentences.i: The woman went back inconsolable, but the dream showed her the old woman’s hut again.
sentences.n: “trostlos” — without Trost, comfort; the adjective stands first and does the work of an adverb, as German adjectives freely do. “der Alten” is the genitive of die Alte, the old woman.

sentences.t: Abermals machte sie sich am nächsten Morgen auf den Weg und klagte der weisen Frau ihr Leid.
sentences.l: Once again she set herself on the way the next morning and lamented her sorrow to the wise woman.
sentences.i: Once again she set out the next morning and poured out her sorrow to the wise woman.
sentences.n: “sich auf den Weg machen” — to set out. “jemandem sein Leid klagen” is fixed: to pour out one’s troubles to someone. Here “weise” is the adjective, wise — die weise Frau, the wise woman, a healer and knower; it is not the noun Weise, a way or manner.

sentences.t: Die Alte gab ihr eine goldene Flöte, und sprach „harre bis der Vollmond wieder kommt, dann nimm diese Flöte, setze dich an das Ufer, blas ein schönes Lied darauf, und wenn du damit fertig bist, so lege sie auf den Sand; du wirst sehen was geschieht.“
sentences.l: The old woman gave her a golden flute and spoke: “wait until the full moon comes again, then take this flute, sit down at the bank, blow a beautiful song on it, and when you are finished with it, lay it on the sand; you will see what happens.”
sentences.i: The old woman gave her a golden flute and said: “Wait until the full moon comes again, then take this flute, sit down on the bank, play a beautiful song on it, and when you have finished, lay it on the sand; you will see what happens.”
sentences.n: “Flöte” here is the noun, a flute, and “blas” the imperative of blasen, to blow — German blows a flute where English plays it. The instruction repeats the first almost word for word with the object changed, and that repetition is the shape of the whole tale.

sentences.t: Die Frau that wie die Alte gesagt hatte.
sentences.l: The woman did as the old woman had said.
sentences.n: “that” is the 1857 spelling of tat, from thun (modern tun).

sentences.t: Kaum lag die Flöte auf dem Sand, so brauste es aus der Tiefe: eine Welle erhob sich, zog heran, und führte die Flöte mit sich fort.
sentences.l: Hardly did the flute lie on the sand when there was a roaring out of the deep: a wave rose up, drew near, and carried the flute away with it.
sentences.i: Hardly was the flute lying on the sand when a roaring came out of the deep: a wave rose, drew near, and carried the flute away with it.
sentences.n: “Kaum …, so …” again — hardly, when. The wording deliberately echoes the first attempt; only “zog heran” is new, where the wave rolled before.

sentences.t: Bald darauf theilte sich das Wasser und nicht bloß der Kopf auch der Mann bis zur Hälfte des Leibes stieg hervor.
sentences.l: Soon after, the water parted and not merely the head, but the man as far as the half of his body rose forth.
sentences.i: Soon afterwards the water parted, and not the head alone but the man as far as the waist rose out of it.
sentences.n: “nicht bloß … auch” — not merely … but also, with the usual sondern left out. Each attempt brings up more of him: head, half the body, and at last the whole man.

sentences.t: Er breitete voll Verlangen seine Arme nach ihr aus, aber eine zweite Welle rauschte heran, bedeckte ihn und zog ihn wieder hinab.
sentences.l: He spread his arms out toward her full of longing, but a second wave came rushing up, covered him and drew him down again.
sentences.i: Full of longing he spread his arms out toward her, but a second wave came rushing up, covered him, and drew him down again.
sentences.n: “ausbreiten” splits right across the clause — breitete … aus, with everything else in between. Verlangen is longing, the noun of verlangen, to crave or demand.

sentences.t: „Ach, was hilft es mir,“ sagte die Unglückliche, „daß ich meinen Liebsten nur erblicke, um ihn wieder zu verlieren.“
sentences.l: “Ah, what use is it to me,” said the unfortunate woman, “that I catch sight of my beloved only to lose him again.”
sentences.i: “Ah, what good does it do me,” said the unhappy woman, “to catch sight of my beloved only to lose him again?”
sentences.n: “die Unglückliche” is the adjective unglücklich used as a noun, and feminine: the unfortunate woman. “um … zu” — in order to, here with the bitter force of ‘only to’.

sentences.t: Der Gram erfüllte aufs neue ihr Herz, aber der Traum führte sie zum drittenmal in das Haus der Alten.
sentences.l: Grief filled her heart anew, but the dream led her for the third time into the house of the old woman.
sentences.i: Grief filled her heart afresh, but the dream led her a third time to the old woman’s house.
sentences.n: “zum drittenmal” — for the third time; in these tales the third attempt is the one that carries.

sentences.t: Sie machte sich auf den Weg, und die weise Frau gab ihr ein goldenes Spinnrad, tröstete sie und sprach „es ist noch nicht alles vollbracht, harre bis der Vollmond kommt, dann nimm das Spinnrad, setze dich an das Ufer und spinn die Spuhle voll, und wenn du fertig bist, so stelle das Spinnrad nahe an das Wasser und du wirst sehen was geschieht.“
sentences.l: She set out on the way, and the wise woman gave her a golden spinning-wheel, comforted her and spoke: “not everything is accomplished yet, wait until the full moon comes, then take the spinning-wheel, sit down at the bank and spin the spool full, and when you are finished, set the spinning-wheel close to the water and you will see what happens.”
sentences.i: She set out, and the wise woman gave her a golden spinning-wheel, comforted her, and said: “Not everything is accomplished yet. Wait until the full moon comes, then take the spinning-wheel, sit down on the bank and spin the spool full, and when you have finished, set the spinning-wheel close to the water, and you will see what happens.”
sentences.n: “stelle” is the imperative of stellen, to set a thing upright — not die Stelle, a place. “die Spuhle” (modern Spule) is the bobbin the spun thread winds onto, and spinning it full is a night’s work: the last gift asks the most of her.

sentences.t: Die Frau befolgte alles genau.
sentences.l: The woman followed everything exactly.
sentences.i: The woman did everything exactly as she had been told.
sentences.n: “befolgen” is to follow instructions, as against folgen, to follow a person.

sentences.t: Sobald der Vollmond sich zeigte, trug sie das goldene Spinnrad an das Ufer und spann emsig bis der Flachs zu Ende und die Spuhle mit dem Faden ganz angefüllt war.
sentences.l: As soon as the full moon showed itself, she carried the golden spinning-wheel to the bank and spun busily until the flax was at an end and the spool was quite filled up with the thread.
sentences.i: As soon as the full moon showed itself, she carried the golden spinning-wheel to the bank and spun busily until the flax was at an end and the spool quite full of thread.
sentences.n: One “war” at the end of the clause serves both halves — German lets it do double duty where English must repeat the verb or recast. Flax is spun steadily and slowly from the distaff, which is why this is the last of the three tasks.

sentences.t: Kaum aber stand das Rad am Ufer, so brauste es noch heftiger als sonst in der Tiefe des Wassers, eine mächtige Welle eilte herbei und trug das Rad mit sich fort.
sentences.l: But hardly did the wheel stand on the bank when it roared in the deep of the water more violently than usual; a mighty wave hurried up and carried the wheel away with it.
sentences.i: But hardly was the wheel standing on the bank when the roaring in the depths of the water came more violently than before; a mighty wave hurried up and carried the wheel away with it.
sentences.n: The third time the same sentence returns enlarged: the roaring is heftiger, the wave mächtig, and it hurries rather than rolls.

sentences.t: Alsbald stieg mit einem Wasserstrahl der Kopf und der ganze Leib des Mannes in die Höhe.
sentences.l: At once, with a jet of water, the head and the whole body of the man rose up on high.
sentences.i: At once, on a jet of water, the man’s head and his whole body rose into the air.
sentences.n: “alsbald” is an elevated ‘at once, straightway’. The series of risings is complete here: head, then half, and now the whole man.

sentences.t: Schnell sprang er ans Ufer, faßte seine Frau an der Hand und entfloh.
sentences.l: Quickly he sprang to the bank, seized his wife by the hand and fled.
sentences.i: He sprang quickly to the bank, caught his wife by the hand, and fled.
sentences.n: “an der Hand fassen” — to take by the hand; German uses an with the dative where English says ‘by’.

sentences.t: Aber kaum hatten sie sich eine kleine Strecke entfernt, so erhob sich mit entsetzlichem Brausen der ganze Weiher und strömte mit reißender Gewalt in das weite Feld hinein.
sentences.l: But hardly had they removed themselves a small distance when the whole pond rose up with dreadful roaring and streamed with tearing force out into the wide field.
sentences.i: But hardly had they gone a little way when the whole pond rose up with a dreadful roar and poured with tearing force out over the open field.
sentences.n: “sich entfernen” — to remove oneself, to get away. “reißende Gewalt” is the force of a torrent, from reißen, to tear. The pond now does whole what the waves had been doing piecemeal.

sentences.t: Schon sahen die Fliehenden ihren Tod vor Augen, da rief die Frau in ihrer Angst die Hilfe der Alten an, und in dem Augenblick waren sie verwandelt, sie in eine Kröte, er in einen Frosch.
sentences.l: Already the fleeing ones saw their death before their eyes; then the woman in her fear called upon the help of the old woman, and in that moment they were transformed, she into a toad, he into a frog.
sentences.i: Already the fleeing pair saw death before their eyes; then the woman in her terror called on the old woman for help, and in that moment they were transformed, she into a toad and he into a frog.
sentences.n: “die Fliehenden” — the fleeing ones, a participle used as a noun. “anrufen” is to call upon for help; separable, rief … an. The same stroke saves them and separates them: neither shape can drown, and neither can hold the other.

sentences.t: Die Flut, die sie erreicht hatte, konnte sie nicht tödten, aber sie riß sie beide von einander und führte sie weit weg.
sentences.l: The flood, which had reached them, could not kill them, but it tore them both from one another and carried them far away.
sentences.i: The flood that overtook them could not kill them, but it tore the two of them apart and carried them far away.
sentences.n: “von einander reißen” — to tear from one another. Three sie in one sentence do three different jobs — the flood, the pair, the flood again; German sorts them by case and position, English has to name them.

sentences.t: Als das Wasser sich verlaufen hatte und beide wieder den trocknen Boden berührten, so kam ihre menschliche Gestalt zurück.
sentences.l: When the water had run away and both touched the dry ground again, their human form came back.
sentences.i: When the water had drained away and the two of them touched dry ground again, their human shape came back.
sentences.n: “sich verlaufen” of water is to run off, to drain away; said of a person, the same verb means to lose one’s way.

sentences.t: Aber keiner wußte wo das andere geblieben war; sie befanden sich unter fremden Menschen, die ihre Heimat nicht kannten.
sentences.l: But neither knew where the other had got to; they found themselves among strange people who did not know their homeland.
sentences.i: But neither knew what had become of the other; they found themselves among strangers who did not know their home country.
sentences.n: “wo … geblieben war” — where the other had remained: German’s way of asking what has become of someone. “kannten” is kennen, to be acquainted with, as against wissen, to know a fact.

sentences.t: Hohe Berge und tiefe Thäler lagen zwischen ihnen.
sentences.l: High mountains and deep valleys lay between them.
sentences.n: “Thäler” is the 1857 spelling of Täler, the plural of Thal (Tal), a valley. Here “tiefe” is the adjective deep — not die Tiefe, the deep, that the waves rose out of a page ago.

sentences.t: Um sich das Leben zu erhalten mußten beide die Schafe hüten.
sentences.l: In order to keep life for themselves both had to tend sheep.
sentences.i: To keep themselves alive, both of them had to tend sheep.
sentences.n: “sich das Leben erhalten” — to keep life for oneself, to make a living. Sheep-tending is the meanest work in these tales, and it is what the huntsman and his wife come down to.

sentences.t: Sie trieben lange Jahre ihre Herden durch Feld und Wald und waren voll Trauer und Sehnsucht.
sentences.l: For long years they drove their flocks through field and wood and were full of mourning and longing.
sentences.i: For long years they drove their flocks through field and wood, full of mourning and longing.
sentences.n: “Herden” here is the flocks they drive — die Herde, a flock or herd, and nothing to do with der Herd, a hearth. “Feld und Wald” is another fixed pair, kept as the doublet it is.

sentences.t: Als wieder einmal der Frühling aus der Erde hervorgebrochen war, zogen beide an einem Tag mit ihren Herden aus und der Zufall wollte daß sie einander entgegen zogen.
sentences.l: When spring had once again broken forth out of the earth, both set out on one day with their flocks, and chance willed that they moved toward one another.
sentences.i: When spring had once again broken out of the earth, the two of them set out on the same day with their flocks, and chance would have it that they moved toward each other.
sentences.n: “der Zufall wollte daß …” — chance willed that; German makes chance the one that wants something. “ausziehen” splits — zogen … aus — and the same verb ziehen returns in “entgegen zogen”, moved toward.

sentences.t: Er erblickte an einem fernen Bergesabhang eine Herde und trieb seine Schafe nach der Gegend hin.
sentences.l: He caught sight of a flock on a distant mountain slope and drove his sheep toward that quarter.
sentences.i: He caught sight of a flock on a distant mountain slope and drove his sheep off in that direction.
sentences.n: “nach der Gegend hin treiben” — to drive toward that region; the little hin at the end says the movement goes away from us. Bergesabhang keeps an old genitive -es inside the compound.

sentences.t: Sie kamen in einem Thal zusammen, aber sie erkannten sich nicht, doch freuten sie sich daß sie nicht mehr so einsam waren.
sentences.l: They came together in a valley, but they did not recognize each other; yet they were glad that they were no longer so alone.
sentences.i: They came together in a valley, but did not know each other; yet they were glad that they were no longer so alone.
sentences.n: “sich erkennen” — the reflexive can be reciprocal, one another rather than oneself, and only the sense tells you which. The tale never explains why they fail to know each other, and does not need to.

sentences.t: Von nun an trieben sie jeden Tag ihre Herde neben einander: sie sprachen nicht viel, aber sie fühlten sich getröstet.
sentences.l: From now on they drove their flock beside one another every day: they did not speak much, but they felt themselves comforted.
sentences.i: From then on they drove their flocks side by side every day: they did not speak much, but they felt comforted.
sentences.n: “Von nun an” — from now on, though the tale stands in the past. “sich getröstet fühlen” — to feel oneself comforted, with a reflexive English drops.

sentences.t: Eines Abends, als der Vollmond am Himmel schien und die Schafe schon ruhten, holte der Schäfer die Flöte aus seiner Tasche und blies ein schönes aber trauriges Lied.
sentences.l: One evening, when the full moon shone in the sky and the sheep were already at rest, the shepherd fetched the flute out of his bag and blew a beautiful but sorrowful song.
sentences.i: One evening, when the full moon shone in the sky and the sheep were already at rest, the shepherd took the flute out of his bag and played a beautiful but sorrowful song.
sentences.n: The full moon and the flute come back together, and the tale says nothing about how he still has it: the objects do the remembering for these two. “Eines Abends” is the genitive of time once more.

sentences.t: Als er fertig war, bemerkte er daß die Schäferin bitterlich weinte.
sentences.l: When he was finished, he noticed that the shepherdess was weeping bitterly.
sentences.n: “Schäferin” is the feminine of Schäfer: German marks the shepherdess with the ending -in, as it does most trades.

sentences.t: „Warum weinst du?“ fragte er.
sentences.l: “Why are you weeping?” he asked.
sentences.n: The first words the two have exchanged since the pond, and they are du — the familiar form, from someone he takes for a stranger.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ antwortete sie, „so schien auch der Vollmond als ich zum letztenmal dieses Lied auf der Flöte blies und das Haupt meines Liebsten aus dem Wasser hervorkam.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” she answered, “so shone the full moon too when I last blew this song on the flute and the head of my beloved came forth out of the water.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” she answered, “the full moon shone just so when I last played this song on the flute and my beloved’s head came out of the water.”
sentences.n: “zum letztenmal” — for the last time. She tells him his own story without knowing it, and the recognition comes through the song rather than the face.

sentences.t: Er sah sie an und es war ihm als fiele eine Decke von den Augen, er erkannte seine liebste Frau: und als sie ihn anschaute und der Mond auf sein Gesicht schien, erkannte sie ihn auch.
sentences.l: He looked at her and it was to him as if a covering fell from his eyes; he recognized his dearest wife: and when she looked at him and the moon shone on his face, she recognized him too.
sentences.i: He looked at her, and it seemed to him as if a veil fell from his eyes; he knew his dearest wife again — and when she looked at him and the moon shone on his face, she knew him too.
sentences.n: “als fiele” is the subjunctive after ‘as if’, with the wenn simply left out — a compact turn German makes often. “es war ihm” — it was to him, the dative used for the person a thing seems to.

sentences.t: Sie umarmten und küßten sich, und ob sie glückselig waren braucht keiner zu fragen.
sentences.l: They embraced and kissed each other, and whether they were blissfully happy nobody needs to ask.
sentences.i: They embraced and kissed, and whether they were happy no one need ask.
sentences.n: The teller steps forward in the last clause and speaks in his own person — “braucht keiner zu fragen”, nobody needs to ask. “ob” here is ‘whether’, not the conditional ‘if’.

glossary.alte: alt — old; die Alte — the old woman (‘eine Alte mit weißen Haaren’)
glossary.alten: alt — old (inflected); substantivized here: die Alte — the old woman (‘die Hütte der Alten’)
glossary.arm: arm — poor (adjective: ‘so arm wäre’ = was so poor)
glossary.arme: arm — poor (adj., inflected: ‘die arme Frau’); also die Arme — arms (pl. of der Arm: ‘seine Arme’)
glossary.armen: der Arm — arms (dat. pl.: ‘mit ihren nassen Armen’); also arm — poor (inflected)
glossary.blitz: der Blitz — lightning (‘wie vom Blitz gerührt’ = as if struck by lightning)
glossary.dar: darbieten — to offer, present itself (separable particle dar-, standing at the end)
glossary.erfüllte: erfüllen — filled (3rd sg. past: ‘der Gram erfüllte ihr Herz’ = grief filled her heart)
glossary.erhalten: erhalten — to keep, to preserve (infinitive: ‘sich das Leben erhalten’ = to keep oneself alive); the same verb elsewhere means to receive
glossary.folge: die Folge — following, compliance (‘Folge leisten’ + dat. = to comply with, to act on)
glossary.freie: das Freie — the open, open country (‘ins Freie’ = out into the open); from frei, free
glossary.fügte: hinzufügen — added (3rd sg. past: ‘fügte er hinzu’; separable hinzu-)
glossary.gut: das Gut — property, goods (‘Geld und Gut’); also gut — good
glossary.hascht: haschen — snatches, seizes (3rd sg. present: ‘hascht dich’ = snatches you)
glossary.herde: die Herde — herd, flock (not der Herd, a hearth)
glossary.hinzu: hinzu — in addition (here the particle of hinzufügen, to add: ‘fügte er hinzu’ = he added)
glossary.kehrte: kehren — turned, returned (3rd sg. past; here with particles: ‘kehrte … ein’ = turned in, ‘kehrte zurück’ = returned)
glossary.lehre: die Lehre — apprenticeship (‘in die Lehre kommen’ = to be apprenticed); also teaching, lesson
glossary.leibes: der Leib — body (gen. sg.: ‘bis zur Hälfte des Leibes’)
glossary.leichter: leicht — lighter (comparative: ‘es wird ihm leichter ums Herz’ = his heart grows lighter); elsewhere: more easily
glossary.liebsten: der Liebste — the beloved, the sweetheart (acc./gen.; from lieb, dear)
glossary.rauschen: rauschen — to rush, to murmur (infinitive; of water)
glossary.schlaf: der Schlaf — sleep (‘in einen tiefen Schlaf’); not the imperative of schlafen
glossary.schrei: der Schrei — cry, scream (‘einen heftigen Schrei ausstoßen’)
glossary.schuld: die Schuld — debt, what one owes (‘an seine Schuld mahnen’ = to press him for what he owes); the same word also means guilt, fault
glossary.setze: setzen — set, place (imperative sg.: ‘setze dich nieder’ = sit yourself down)
glossary.stelle: stellen — set, place (imperative sg.: ‘stelle das Spinnrad’)
glossary.tiefe: die Tiefe — the deep, the depths (‘aus der Tiefe’); also tief — deep (adj., ‘tiefe Thäler’)
glossary.trocknen: trocken — dry (adj., inflected: ‘den trocknen Boden’ = the dry ground); not the verb trocknen, to dry
glossary.unglückliche: unglücklich — unhappy, ill-fated; substantivized die Unglückliche — the unfortunate woman
glossary.verlaufen: verlaufen — run off, drained away (past part.; ‘das Wasser hatte sich verlaufen’); said of a person, sich verlaufen is to lose one’s way
glossary.wagen: wagen — to venture, to dare (infinitive; ‘sich wagen’ = to venture oneself somewhere)
glossary.weib: das Weib — woman (here the older plain word, without the contempt it later took on)
glossary.weise: weise — wise (adjective); also die Weise — way, manner
glossary.zogen: ziehen — drew, moved (3rd pl. past; here with particles: ‘zogen … aus’ = set out, ‘entgegen zogen’ = moved toward one another)
